ML Ratchet · physics + machine learning · project 6

SwellCast

A storm thousands of kilometres away sends swell to a buoy. Long waves travel faster than short ones, so they arrive first, and the frequency at the buoy climbs in a straight line, df/dt = g / 4πD. Walter Munk used that slope in 1963 to find storms nobody had seen. SwellCast is a small neural network that reads the slope, the timing and the direction from ten days of a real buoy’s wave spectra. It was trained only on simulated swell laid on top of real buoy records, then tested on hurricanes and typhoons it never saw.

Real arrivals, exam set

What the buoy recorded

Each picture is ten days at one NOAA buoy. Up is wave frequency, right is time, colour is wave energy. A distant storm shows up as a tilted streak: low frequencies (long periods) first. The dashed line is where the streak should sit if you know the real storm (from the IBTrACS best track). The network runs here in your browser on the same numbers. These 12 events are a fixed random draw from the exam, stratified by ocean basin; none were picked by result.

Lab

Make a storm

Click the map to put a storm somewhere in the ocean, then use the sliders to change its wave height, size, duration and timing. The page simulates its swell with the same physics used for training (a JONSWAP sea that grows and decays, spreading over the sphere, air-friction loss on the way) and adds it to a real quiet ten-day record from 2025. The network then reads the result. Make the storm weak or far and watch the streak flatten and fade into the background.

Real storms it never saw

The ratchet

Every change, kept or not

A change is kept only if it raises the score on a frozen set of simulated buoy windows by more than 0.01 (mean skill over distance, timing, direction, storm size and detection) and does not make the 29 real development arrivals more than 5% worse. The exam is computed for every rung but never used to choose.
